AARON ALDERMAN / AUTHOR

A world someone else can enter.

On attention, imagination and the responsibility of shaping a story.

A personal essay · A working reflection, open to correction

A story begins with a choice about what to notice. A gesture can become an opening; a silence can change a scene; a detail that looked incidental can ask to be seen again. I want to stay with that attention before deciding what the story must mean.

The Author side of this world is about shaping an experience another person can enter. It includes the pleasure of making things up and the responsibility of knowing when invention, interpretation and an account of real events need different labels.

IN THIS ESSAY

  1. Attend to a life before turning it into a story.
  2. Give the invented world something to resist.
  3. Invite a reader without assigning them a private story.
  4. Let beauty and humour have room to work.
  5. Let revision change what I thought the story was.
  6. Compose a world that remains open.

01

Attend to a life before turning it into a story.

A person can exceed the role a plot offers them. I want to ask what a scene leaves outside the frame: another point of view, an ordinary need, a relationship that does not exist simply to advance the central character.

When a story draws on real life, the ability to describe someone does not give me unlimited authority over their account. I need to consider what is mine to tell, what requires permission and where a faithful uncertainty belongs.

I can also choose a more general scene when a lesson does not need a private history. That distance can give a reader room to recognise something without requiring them to inherit the author’s circumstances or conclusions.

02

Give the invented world something to resist.

Imagination can make room for a possibility that ordinary habits have hidden. A world becomes more interesting when its relationships and consequences have enough shape that an easy answer cannot resolve everything.

I want the work to keep track of what its choices cost. A character’s action should meet the world and the other people in it. A beautiful setting can deepen that encounter when it offers something to explore, rather than only decorating an explanation.

Fiction can make an emotional or ethical possibility intelligible. Its power to move a reader does not turn an invented event into historical evidence. Naming the kind of work being offered protects both imagination and truth.

03

Invite a reader without assigning them a private story.

A reader brings experiences I cannot know. I can offer a question, a scene or a change in perspective without telling them what they secretly fear or what a chosen route proves about their character.

I like the possibility that the same scene can mean something different on return. An earlier detail can acquire weight because the reader has encountered another relationship or point of view. The story can invite that recognition and leave its personal meaning with them.

A branching world makes this responsibility more visible. Choosing a route should give a reader a meaningful way to explore. It should not disguise an assessment of their worth as a playful interaction.

04

Let beauty and humour have room to work.

A story does not need to explain every image immediately. A small joke can release pressure; an odd detail can invite a second look; a quiet stretch can let the reader’s attention settle somewhere the argument did not predict.

I want beauty to be part of that invitation. Colour, rhythm, space and movement can help a world feel inhabited. They also need to serve the reading: a sentence should remain readable, an action recognisable and an unfamiliar idea approachable.

The pleasure of the work can carry a serious question without turning every encounter into instruction. Sometimes the reader needs a little space to discover the connection themselves.

05

Let revision change what I thought the story was.

Revision can begin with a sentence and reach the frame around it. Whose account became too convenient? Which consequence did I avoid? Does the scene invite attention, or keep pressing the reader toward the response I wanted?

I want to distinguish what a reader actually says from my interpretation of their response. Disagreement may reveal a weakness, a different experience or a live tension the story should preserve. It does not have to be converted into a single measure of success.

A faithful draft can become clearer without becoming less particular. Sometimes the better change is to remove a claim I cannot support, leave an uncertainty visible or allow a character more room than the first outline gave them.

06

Compose a world that remains open.

Worldwright is the developing platform for this kind of storytelling: a composition whose scenes, relationships and routes can be inspected. The present site is one evolving use of that idea, with working examples and unfinished joins.

The ambition is for an author to shape a coherent world while a reader finds a journey within it. Reusable structure can support that freedom, provided the structure does not mistake a record of navigation for an account of someone’s inner life.

The question I want beside the next draft is generous and exacting: what can another person discover here that I have made room for, but have not already decided on their behalf?

A question beside the next draft

Whose point of view is missing, what kind of truth am I claiming, and where can the reader make a connection of their own?
